question: Does Workday (NASDAQ: WDAY) report a gross or net retention metric in its annual or quarterly reporting? If so, provide the definition
answer:
Workday tracks and reports on Gross Revenue Retention Rate. 

The company defines Gross Revenue Retention Rate as the percentage of recurring revenue retained from existing customers and is calculated by taking total annual recurring revenue (“ARR”) of our customers as of the corresponding prior period-end and comparing that to ARR from that same set of customers as of the current period-end. The metric takes into account recurring revenues lost to product or customer churn but does not account for additional revenue earned from add-ons or net expansions, which include volume and price adjustments.

model_answer:
## Short answer

**Yes — Workday reports a gross metric ("gross revenue retention rate," or GRR) and has stopped reporting a net retention metric.** It discloses GRR in the MD&A section of both its Form 10-K and Form 10-Q (and repeats the definition in its investor presentations). Net revenue retention ("net revenue retention rate") was disclosed only qualitatively (>100%) through late 2024 and was then dropped entirely after SEC comment-letter engagement.

## The current disclosure (verbatim, FY2026 10-K, filed March 6, 2026)

> **Gross Revenue Retention Rate**
>
> "Our growth in subscription services revenues attributable to existing customers is further reflected by our **gross revenue retention rate of approximately 97% as of January 31, 2026**. Our gross revenue retention rate measures the percentage of recurring revenue retained from existing customers and is calculated by taking total annual recurring revenue ("ARR") of our customers as of the corresponding prior period-end and comparing that to ARR from that same set of customers as of the current period-end. The metric takes into account recurring revenues lost to product or customer churn but does not account for additional revenue earned from add-ons or net expansions, which include volume and price adjustments. Our high gross revenue retention rate demonstrates our ability to maintain our existing customer base and drive strong overall customer satisfaction.
>
> Our gross revenue retention rate is based on ARR, which represents the annualized value of active subscription contracts as of the end of each period. Each subscription contract is annualized by dividing the total contract value by the number of days in the contract term and then multiplying by 365. We exclude certain subscription contracts from the calculation, including contracts with terms less than one year that are distinct from our core product offering, such as contracts for tenants which are used for implementation and testing. To the extent that we are negotiating a renewal with a customer after the expiration of the subscription, ARR is only adjusted if the customer churns. We calculate ARR on a constant currency basis using exchange rates set at the beginning of each fiscal year."

The same identical language appears in the Q2 FY2027 10-Q (quarter ended July 31, 2026), which states GRR "**of approximately 97% as of July 31, 2026**," and in the FY2025 10-K ("**approximately 98%** as of January 31, 2025"). Note that the definition is a *same-cohort* comparison (ARR for the exact set of customers existing at the prior period-end, measured again at the current period-end) — the point the SEC specifically asked Workday to clarify.

## Why there's no net retention metric anymore

- **Through FY2024 and the first three quarters of FY2025**, Workday said only that gross and net revenue retention rates "exceeded 95% and 100%, respectively," without publishing figures.
- **SEC comment letters (Aug.–Sept. 2024)** pushed the company to give actual numbers and to explain the cohort mechanics.
- **Workday's September 19, 2024 response letter** committed to two changes:
  1. *"…we no longer intend to include disclosure related to net revenue retention rates in our SEC filings… the net revenue retention rate is largely duplicative of the change in revenue from existing customers."* Instead, it now discloses **the percentage change in subscription revenue attributable to existing vs. new customers** (e.g., in FY2026: ~60% of the subscription revenue increase came from customers existing at the start of the prior year, ~40% from new customers).
  2. *"…we currently intend to continue disclosing our gross revenue retention rate in future filings… we plan to disclose the actual, then-current gross revenue retention rate for each period."*
- Notably, Workday told the staff it **does not consider gross or net retention to be key performance indicators** and does not use them in managing the business — they are "supplemental data" only.

## Practical notes for modeling

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Metric name | Gross revenue retention rate (GRR), ARR-based, constant currency |
| Where disclosed | Item 7 MD&A of 10-K and 10-Q; investor presentation footnotes |
| Precision | "Approximately" a whole percent (97%, 98%) — no basis points |
| Recent values | ~98% (Jan 31, 2025), ~97% (Jan 31, 2026), ~97% (Jul 31, 2026) |
| Net retention | Not disclosed; no numeric NRR has ever been published |
| Substitute metric | % of subscription revenue growth from existing vs. new customers |

One caution: because GRR excludes price/volume expansions by construction, Workday's ~97% is not comparable to net-dollar-retention figures quoted for other SaaS companies, and several third-party data aggregators have historically mixed the two series together — worth checking the underlying filing language rather than a scraped KPI table.
